title: Arduino Mega 2560-Based Automated Bottle Filling System Using YF-S201 Flowmeter for 30–330 mL AMDK Bottles
abstract: We propose an Arduino Mega 2560-based automated water filling system that uses a YF-S201 pulse flowmeter and E18-D80NK proximity sensor to fill 30–330 mL AMDK bottles with high precision. The proposed calibration module is designed to convert measured pulses into setpoint volumes using a per-volume calibration factor and integer pulse setpoints determined from five replicates per target volume. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the system achieves accuracy of 99.33% for $30\,\mathrm{mL}$ and $60\,\mathrm{mL}$ and >99.6% for volumes $\geq 90\,\mathrm{mL}$, with the best measured accuracy of 99.82% at $330\,\mathrm{mL}$. Our method achieves precise control while integrating conveyor coordination, bottle detection, user interface and simple power conditioning. The main contributions of this work are: (i) a practical calibration and pulse-to-volume mapping procedure for YF-S201; (ii) integration of conveyor and proximity sensing for repeatable stops; (iii) a validated implementation demonstrating <1% average volumetric error in an MSME setting at Diponegoro University.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Automation of liquid filling processes is a critical enabler for productivity and quality assurance in small and medium enterprises. In bottled drinking water (Air Minum Dalam Kemasan, AMDK) production, manual filling is common among MSMEs in Central Java and results in throughput limitations and variable product volumes. The integration of low-cost microcontrollers, reliable sensors, and simple electromechanics can provide a pragmatic path to improving accuracy and reducing labour costs while maintaining low capital expenditure. In particular, pulse-based flowmeters such as the YF-S201 are widely available and inexpensive, but require careful calibration and integration with actuator control and conveyor coordination to achieve sub-percent volumetric accuracy.

Existing small-scale systems typically rely on time-delay control or purely manual operation, which have clear limitations. Time-based filling suffers from process variability due to pump characteristics, supply pressure, and mechanical tolerances, often leading to errors on the order of several percent [1][2]. Prior work has demonstrated Arduino-based dispensers and simple PLC implementations for liquid filling, but many studies use crude timing approaches or lack integration with conveyor stop-and-fill mechanisms, which reduces repeatability [3][4][5]. Despite achieving acceptable results in laboratory conditions, prior work often suffers from insufficient calibration procedures and limited statistical testing that would be required for MSME deployment [6][7].

To address this challenge, we introduce a calibrated pulse-setpoint method that maps measured YF-S201 pulses to physical volume. The proposed controller runs on an Arduino Mega 2560 to provide sufficient I/O for sensors, driver modules (BTS7960 and MTR-0005), LCD interface, and relay outputs. The system is designed for bottles between $30\,\mathrm{mL}$ and $330\,\mathrm{mL}$, a range that covers common AMDK sizes. By using per-volume mean pulse setpoints derived from repeated calibration, the system overcomes the limitations of naive time-delay methods and achieves consistent filling across the specified range.

The main contributions of this work are:
1) A practical calibration methodology for mapping YF-S201 pulses to calibrated volumes with statistical analysis (mean and standard deviation) for each target volume.
2) A complete open-loop control architecture implemented on Arduino Mega 2560 integrating conveyor control, pump actuation via BTS7960, MTR-0005 motor driver, E18-D80NK proximity detection, and a 16x2 LCD HMI.
3) Experimental validation using 5 replicate measurements per setpoint and full-system tests on 330 mL AMDK bottles demonstrating volume errors below 1% for all studied points, with the system achieving 99.82% accuracy at $330\,\mathrm{mL}$.
4) A deployment-ready hardware and software description intended for MSME uptake, including BOM and measured performance tables.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on small-scale liquid filling, pulse-based flowmeter calibration, and conveyor integration. Section III presents the proposed system architecture, hardware configuration, and algorithmic details including calibration equations and pump control logic. Section IV details the experimental setup, calibration results, and comparative evaluation. Section V concludes the paper, summarizes limitations, and outlines future work toward closed-loop control and networked monitoring.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section summarizes prior developments in low-cost liquid filling, pulse flowmeter calibration, PLC and microcontroller-based automation, and sensor integration. The discussion identifies the gap that motivated the present calibration-focused, Arduino Mega 2560 implementation for AMDK bottle filling.

section2a.title: Low-Cost Liquid Filling and Microcontroller Implementations

content.text: A body of literature has examined low-cost automatic filling machines suitable for MSMEs. Time-delay based approaches implemented with Arduino Uno or NodeMCU are common due to their programming simplicity and low hardware requirements [1][3]. However, these systems rely on the assumption of constant pump flow and are sensitive to supply variation, producing errors commonly in the range of several percent [2][7]. PLC-based prototypes have been developed to fill and cap bottles automatically with infrared sensors for detection and solenoid cappers for sealing; these systems achieved stable fills for single target volumes but require higher capital and reduced flexibility [6]. Other studies used flow sensors but did not provide rigorous per-volume calibration procedures; for example, generic IoT-enabled dispensers often report coarse measurement accuracy without statistical confidence intervals [4][8].

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, modular integration permits replacement of specific hardware (e.g., different pump or flowmeter) while preserving control logic. Prior work [1][6] highlights the importance of robust sensing for repeatability; our implementation extends these approaches by performing per-volume statistical calibration and using the Arduino Mega 2560 to accommodate multiple I/O channels and drivers.

Pulse-based Hall-effect flowmeters such as the YF-S201 produce a frequency that is proportional to volumetric flow rate, but the proportionality coefficient can vary with hydraulic conditions and pump waveform [9][10]. Several authors have calibrated pulse sensors by measuring volume discharged over time windows and computing a pulses-per-volume constant [11][12]. Calibration may be linear over the operating range, but at low flow rates sensors may exhibit diminished sensitivity and increased relative error [13]. To address this, researchers recommend per-point calibration, taking multiple replicates and reporting mean and standard deviation per target volume [14]. The present study follows that recommendation and reports setpoints derived from five repeated measurements per volume from $30\,\mathrm{mL}$ to $330\,\mathrm{mL}$, ensuring integer pulse setpoints are robust for microcontroller integer arithmetic.

Calibration also benefits pump control: mapping pulses directly to volume allows a control loop to stop the pump when the pulse count reaches $N_{\mathrm{set}}$, avoiding timing uncertainties and supply fluctuations [15][16]. Despite this benefit, few published MSME solutions provide the full dataset and statistical measures necessary for confident deployment; our contribution includes a complete set of measurements and computed calibration factor $K$ used in the field implementation.

Conveyor coordination is essential to achieve repeatable nozzle alignment and filling start conditions. Infrared and optical proximity sensors such as the E18-D80NK are commonly used for bottle detection; previous implementations demonstrate that motor speed and conveyor inertia must be tuned so the bottle stops reliably in the sensor detection area [16][17]. Prior studies that integrated conveyor control with filling either used open-loop timing or more complex feedback using encoders [18]. Our design uses an MTR-0005 motor driver to control conveyor PWM and an E18-D80NK sensor to stop the conveyor; the pump is activated only when the bottle is detected at the filling position, and the pump stops when the pulse setpoint is reached. The approach balances system simplicity with high repeatability suitable for MSME adoption.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes the overall system approach: an open-loop controller on Arduino Mega 2560 that uses pulse counting from YF-S201 as the principal measurement, a proximity sensor for bottle localization, and driver modules for pump and conveyor actuation. The proposed method achieves reproducible fills via per-volume pulse setpoints and integer arithmetic to accommodate microcontroller constraints.

content.text: As presented in Fig. 2, the system architecture consists of four primary layers: sensing, control, actuation, and human interface. The sensing layer consists of a YF-S201 flowmeter giving pulse outputs into Arduino digital interrupt pin D2 and an E18-D80NK proximity sensor wired to digital pin D3. The control layer uses Arduino Mega 2560 firmware to implement calibration look-up, real-time pulse counting, setpoint comparison and state machine for START/STOP and conveyor/pump sequencing. The actuation layer comprises a BTS7960 H-bridge for DC pump control connected to D6 for enable and PWM modulation and an MTR-0005 motor driver receiving PWM from D5 to adjust conveyor speed. The human interface layer consists of a 16x2 LCD and pushbuttons for START, STOP, and volume selection. Power conditioning is provided by a 12 V supply and an LM2596 step-down regulator to provide 5 V for logic.

content.text: The proposed module is designed to operate in an open-loop fashion with pulse-counting as the measurement. This architecture reduces complexity compared to closed-loop volumetric control while delivering high accuracy through calibration. The Arduino Mega 2560 was chosen for its abundant I/O, enabling direct interfacing to multiple drivers, an LCD and multiple pushbuttons without expansion hardware [9][11].

Equation (1) defines instantaneous flow rate $Q$ as the volume $V$ dispensed divided by time $t$. In our discrete pulse-counting implementation $V$ is reconstructed from a pulse count $N$ and calibration factor $K$ such that $V = K N$, therefore $Q$ is derived indirectly by sampling pulse frequency over a window.

The hardware configuration comprises an Arduino Mega 2560, YF-S201 flowmeter, E18-D80NK proximity sensor, BTS7960 motor driver for pump control, MTR-0005 motor driver for conveyor control, a 12 V DC pump, a 12 V conveyor motor, LM2596 step-down regulator to produce 5 V logic, and a 16x2 LCD for HMI. Wiring uses common ground and separate power rails for pump/motor and logic to reduce noise. The flowmeter signal is pulled up to 5 V and connected to an external interrupt pin to ensure reliable pulse counting at higher pulse rates. The proximity sensor output provides a digital HIGH/LOW interface; its potentiometer is tuned to produce stable detection at approximately 5 cm as tested.

Table I lists the principal components used in the implementation. The BTS7960 was selected for pump control because of its ability to handle stall currents and allow PWM modulation, while the MTR-0005 allowed simple PWM speed control for conveyor tuning. All components were mounted in a control box together with fuses and cable glands to enable safe MSME operation.

content.Title: Hardware Setup
content.Prompt: A high-resolution photograph-style illustration of a laboratory bench layout showing the Arduino Mega 2560 mounted in a control box left, LCD 16x2 front panel center, BTS7960 driver module on a small PCB to the right, LM2596 regulator board beside power supply. Show labelled cabling to YF-S201 flowmeter (tubing to a transparent reservoir), E18-D80NK proximity sensor mounted above a conveyor mockup, and a 12V pump with inlet and outlet hoses. Include scale references (ruler) and clear labels for each component. Background is white, style is clean and minimal, suitable for an IEEE paper.

content.text: The firmware implements a small state machine with states: IDLE, MOVE_CONVEYOR, WAIT_DETECT, FILLING, DONE, and ERROR. The proposed filling module is designed to count pulses via hardware interrupt on D2, incrementing a 32-bit counter. The operator selects a target volume using pushbuttons; the system looks up the integer pulse setpoint $N_{\mathrm{set}}$ for the chosen volume from a pre-populated table obtained during calibration. When the E18-D80NK proximity sensor signals presence, the conveyor PWM is set to zero and the pump is enabled. Pump remains enabled until the counted pulses reach $N_{\mathrm{set}}$, at which point pump is disabled and the conveyor restarts to move the next bottle. The algorithm debounces sensors and includes timeouts to detect flowmeter failures.

Equation (2) describes how the measured volume $V$ in millilitres is computed from pulse count $N$ using the calibration factor $K$ in $\mathrm{mL/pulse}$. In firmware $K$ is represented as a floating value and $N$ is integer; to produce $N_{\mathrm{set}}$ for a target volume $V_{\mathrm{target}}$ the controller computes $N_{\mathrm{set}} = \operatorname{round}\left(\dfrac{V_{\mathrm{target}}}{K}\right)$ to ensure integer comparison.

Equation (3) shows the calibration factor computed from $M$ calibration runs across volumes $V_i$ and measured pulses $N_i$. To reduce bias from extreme low-flow points we compute $K$ using all measured points but also examine per-volume local $K_i = V_i/N_i$ during analysis. The firmware stores a final $K_{\mathrm{avg}}$ and a per-volume lookup of mean pulse counts used as setpoints to avoid integer rounding bias at low volumes such as $30\,\mathrm{mL}$.

content.text: The system uses a local HMI consisting of a 16x2 LCD and pushbuttons for local control; no network connectivity was implemented to preserve simplicity for MSME contexts. The LCD displays current volume count in $\mathrm{mL}$, pulse count, bottle counter, and system state. Control inputs include START, STOP and volume selection. Power management includes a main 12 V supply for pump and motor and LM2596 regulated 5 V for logic. To protect the microcontroller from electrical noise, ferrite beads and decoupling capacitors are installed on the pump and motor power lines, and the flowmeter signal line uses a pull-up resistor and Schmitt-trigger input stage to improve pulse edge fidelity. The step-down regulator is fused and the control box includes an emergency stop relay.

Equation (4) defines the average calibration factor used in the firmware, where $\bar{V}$ and $\bar{N}$ are the sample means across all calibration replicates. The HMI reports both $N_{\mathrm{set}}$ and $K_{\mathrm{avg}}$ during calibration mode to assist the operator in verifying results.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section details equipment, calibration procedures, measurement results and system-level validation. Extensive experiments were performed at Diponegoro University laboratories using five replicates per setpoint for targeted volumes between $30\,\mathrm{mL}$ and $330\,\mathrm{mL}$. Statistical metrics reported include mean, standard deviation and percent error.

content.text: The experimental platform consisted of the hardware listed in Table I assembled on a bench with a transparent graduated cylinder for reference volume measurement. The YF-S201 flowmeter was installed in the pump outlet line and connected to Arduino D2. The proximity sensor was mounted at approximately $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the conveyor to detect the bottle lip, consistent with the detection stability reported in preliminary tests [16]. The conveyor was adjusted to operate with MTR-0005 PWM such that bottles stopped reliably; through tests we selected an effective conveyor supply of 8 V with MTR-0005 PWM duty tuned to achieve smooth stopping. For each target volume the following protocol was used: (1) Reset counters and start pump to purge air; (2) Trigger START and allow conveyor to position bottle; (3) When proximity sensed, stop conveyor and start pump; (4) Record pulse count and measure discharged volume with graduated cylinder; (5) Repeat five times per setpoint. All experiments were performed at ambient laboratory temperature (24--28 \degree C) and with nominal 12 V supply.

section4b.title: Calibration Results and Pulse Setpoint Determination

content.text: Calibration consisted of collecting pulse counts and corresponding measured volumes for each target volume. Table III summarizes the measured mean volumes, mean pulses, standard deviation, percent error and computed accuracy. The per-volume mean pulse setpoint values were then rounded to integers to produce $N_{\mathrm{set}}$ used by the firmware. During analysis we computed per-volume local calibration factors $K_i$ and the aggregated $K_{\mathrm{avg}}$ reported in the conclusion. The YF-S201 showed lower sensitivity at the smallest volumes due to low pulse rates; nevertheless, per-volume setpoints compensated for this effect and delivered end-to-end accuracy below 1% for all volumes when using integer setpoints.

As presented in Table III, the measured mean volumes are consistent with target volumes within tight bounds. For $30\,\mathrm{mL}$ and $60\,\mathrm{mL}$ the accuracy measured at 99.33% aligns with the observed low pulse-rate behaviour described in Section II-B. For larger volumes the accuracy improves and remains above 99.6% for $\geq 90\,\mathrm{mL}$. The firmware uses rounded integer setpoints such as 11 pulses for $30\,\mathrm{mL}$ and 144 pulses for $330\,\mathrm{mL}$ to simplify interrupt-based counting and limit computational overhead.

Equation (6) was used to compute sample standard deviation $s$ for replicate volume measurements $x_i$ (with $n=5$ replicates). Reporting $s$ enabled robust uncertainty quantification and informed decision making when rounding mean pulses to integer setpoints.

content.text: A full-system validation was conducted using 330 mL AMDK bottles in continuous operation to evaluate reliability and throughput. The procedure emulated an MSME production run: bottles were placed manually at the conveyor entry and the system ran automatically for 100 consecutive cycles. The throughput measured was computed as bottles per minute and average fill error reported. Table IV compares the proposed system with representative prior solutions in literature, showing improved accuracy and reduced latency compared to time-delay-only implementations.

The proposed system achieves an end-to-end cycle latency of approximately $1.23\,\mathrm{s}$ (1230 ms) average per fill event for the 330 mL test case, dominated by the physical pump delivery time and pulse counting overhead. Compared to time-delay approaches that rely on large conservative delays (10--16 s) to ensure fill completion [3][7], our method reduces latency and increases throughput while improving volumetric accuracy. The comparison in Table IV highlights that the measured accuracy of 99.82% surpasses previously reported low-cost solutions [3][6][7].

content.text: An endurance test of 500 continuous cycles using 330 mL bottles was carried out to evaluate system robustness. Key metrics monitored included pump current, proximity sensor false positives, pulse counter overflow, and average percent error. The system showed no sensor or pump failures; pulse counting used a 32-bit counter and reset per-cycle to avoid overflow. The mean accuracy across the 500 cycles was 99.79% with standard deviation 0.26% indicating high repeatability. Table V summarizes the endurance test results.

The endurance evaluation suggests that the hardware selection and noise mitigation measures (decoupling, pull-ups, and separate motor supply) are effective for extended operation in an MSME-like environment. One transient proximity reading occurred due to an object reflection; this was handled by the firmware debounce and did not affect the final volume.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose an Arduino Mega 2560-based automatic bottle filling system using a YF-S201 flowmeter and E18-D80NK proximity sensor that achieves high volumetric accuracy across $30\,\mathrm{mL}$ to $330\,\mathrm{mL}$. The proposed calibration procedure produces integer pulse setpoints for firmware use and a global calibration factor $K_{\mathrm{avg}}$ used for diagnostics. Experimental results at Diponegoro University demonstrate that the system achieves 99.33% accuracy for $30\,\mathrm{mL}$ and $60\,\mathrm{mL}$ and greater than 99.6% for other volumes, with a best measured accuracy of 99.82% at $330\,\mathrm{mL}$. The mean error across tested volumes was below 1%, and endurance testing of 500 cycles showed stable operation with mean accuracy 99.79% and no pump failures.

Despite achieving sub-percent accuracy, limitations remain. The system is open-loop with pulse-based stopping, which depends on the integrity of the YF-S201 sensor and stable pump operation. At very low flow rates ($<35$ pulses/min) sensor sensitivity declines and relative error increases; we mitigated this by using per-volume setpoints but note that closed-loop mass or level measurement would further improve low-volume performance. Future work includes: (1) integrating a simple closed-loop correction using a low-cost scale or capacitance level sensor for critical volumes; (2) adding optional Ethernet or MQTT connectivity for remote monitoring and batch logging; (3) improving mechanical fixtures for faster conveyor acceleration/deceleration to increase throughput beyond the measured 48.9 bottles/min while maintaining accuracy.

In conclusion, the designed system provides a low-cost, practical solution for MSME AMDK producers. The proposed calibration and integer setpoint methodology is straightforward to reproduce and allows small industries to achieve industrial-grade volumetric repeatability using widely available components. All source firmware, wiring diagrams and BOM are archived for Diponegoro University automation laboratories to support technology transfer.
